speechtext: The House resumed the discussion consequent on the statement made this afternoon by the Right Hon. Sir Robert Borden (Prime Minister) as to the transactions of the Imperial War Cabinet and of .the Imperial War Conference.

maintopic: THE PRIME MINISTER'S VISIT TO ENGLAND.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a word or twoi with regard to what took place this afternoon and in regard to the matters which formed the subject of discussion and which are of the greatest importance to Canada and to the Empire. In the first place, I desire *to congratulate the right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) and the Government on coming to the view that conscription must be resorted to in Canada	in order	that	we	may do	ourfull	share in	this	war. While	the
decision is somewhat delayed. I believe the people of Canada will appreciate the final determination at which the Government has arrived. Certainly this policy will he appreciated in my own province and,
I think, all over the Dominion. The position in the country and in this House might he well expressed by a reference to the recent activities of the ginger party

in Great Britain-the party that demanded that more ginger be put into the conduct of the war.
The result of the ginger movement in the Mother Country was a reorganization of the Cabinet, not only once but twice. New men were taken in, with a policy based on conscription and a more vigorous prosecution of the war, and a determination to do everything that possibly could he done by Parliament to bring the war to a successful conclusion. I take it that the announcement made here to-day means a more vigorous prosecution of the war by this Government. I congratulate the Government on what has been decided in regard to conscription.
The vigorous policy which has been foreshadowed in connection with conscription should also be applied to many other questions in connection with the war. I should have liked to have heard that the Government intended not only to take up vigorously the question of conscription, but also to take up what the ginger party brought in Great Britain, food control, the appointment of a food dictator and a very widespread control of all prices, especially those of the needs of life. The speech of the Prime Minister this afternoon also contained an intimation that more gingeT might be put into the transportation policy of this country. The Prime Minister hinted at a policy that would mean the Government and Parliament of this country taking a more pronounced course in regard to transportation in relation both to railway and ocean traffic. The only effective way of improving transportation facilities is to have some kind of Government control of the railways and of the ocean liners. I shall not be surprised to see a transportation policy adopted by the Parliament of Canada that will produce a great shipping industry in this country, even if the Government have to own the ships. I hope for such a policy and through it we can improve the condition of Canada and of the farmers of Canada who are raising reheat for the Mother Country and the Allies. They have long had Government control of railways in Europe, especially in Germany, and I believe that the United States will have it now that they are in the war, that there will be public ownership of railways, as there now is provision for their absolute control. We shall have to do the same thing here and I hope I was not going too far in assuming from the Prime Min-

ister's speech that we shall have more ginger at least in regard to railway transportation in this country; that the farmers of the West especially will be able to market their grain at lower freight rates, and that they will also obtain relief from the exorbitant tolls charged on freight by the ocean lines.
There are one or two other things in which we want a great deal more ginger in the policy of the Government.

maintopic: THE PRIME MINISTER'S VISIT TO ENGLAND.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: THE PRIME MINISTER'S VISIT TO ENGLAND.
speechtext:
The Prime Minister this afternoon said that he was surprised to learn of the experience of a friend of his who was told in Germany by a business man how much the Germans knew of the stores of iron ore in Belle Isle, off the coast of Newfoundland. The same knowledge that the Germans had of those iron ores in Newfoundland they have always had of the nickle deposits of this country. The time has surely come when we must have a national policy in regard to the control of those great natural resources of Canada and of the Empire. We must have a national policy in regard to our nickle. We must know before this war is over whether it is true that the Krupp Company really controls the nickle deposits of Canada. I believe that information is obtainable in the United States which will verify what has been said, that the nickle deposits of this country, which ought to be consecrated to the Empire and should be controlled by ourselves and used by the Empire, melted and refined in our own country, are controlled by hostile interests. Then we have the greatest asbestos deposits in the world in the province of Quebec. Yet the control of those great deposits is outside of Canada. It is absolutely necessary that we should have control of this product, and we must have some national policy in respect to it. There are two other things, petroleum and gasolene, two absolute necessities of war, two things that can be produced in this country-yet the control of our deposits of these great resources is not in Canada. We have the oil wells in Canada, and we ought not to allow a gallon of gasolene to be consumed in this country which is not refined and distilled within the country. These are things that are essential to war. They are natural products of Canada, and in the case of two or three of them we have a monopoly; yet we have not exercised that monopoly. I say that in this new policy, this progressive policy,
which the Government are announcing to-day, and which tends in a good direction, we must go further and include other lines.
Then, too, we must have a more progressive policy in regard to currency and banking in Canada, a matter to which I have before referred in this House. That is essential in connection with .the war. I hope we shall have an announcement of a more progressive policy in that respect before long. I trust that not only will we have conscription in this country and a far-reaching measure of conscription, but that it will be vigorously presented in this House and vigorously prosecuted and put into force, because the war is not won; it has to ;be won, and everything must be done to win it. There must be absolute c,o-o.peration and unity in this country to win the war, and if a progressive policy is adopted it ought to be supported by a united Parliament, as it will be supported, I believe, by a united people.
'The Prime Minister also dealt with a question about which I have .thought a good deal, that is the rearrangement of the various elements of the Empire and their .standing, one with the other, and how far this war will lead us in the way of com federation or consolidation of our interests. I agree with what the Prime Minister said that he has not very much sympathy with that new school in England called the Bound Table school, who are trying to land the Empire into some system ,of confederation.
I had not a great deal of faith in that. I believe in the principle laid down by Sir John A. Macdonald, and followed by the right hon. Prime Minister this afternoon, that while it is desirable that there should be an alliance and a consultation of governments of the Empire, we must retain our absolute autonomy, our absolute independence, and our right to pass on any question of Imperial policy before we are definitely committed to it. That is an important consideration which should not be discussed at this time but which, when a further conference is held and When the relations of the various parts of the Empire one to the other and to the union are dealt with, will be most carefully considered. I am confident that no step will be taken until each member of the Conference has had an opportunity of discussing it in his own Parliament. I support the Prime Minister in his going to the Conference and taking part in its discussions. His going there had a good effect upon him and he

has come back with what I am quite sure is -a progressive proposition with regard to the conduct of the war.
What I would like the Government to do, now that they have declared for conscription, is to go vigorously into it and do what the United States are doing. Conscription is practically in force there to-day, or will be as soon as the President signs the Bill; they purpose raising a draft of 500,000 men by this method. By employing the same method we can raise 100,000 or 200,000 men, or even more, if we have to-and I beliqye we shall have to. I hope that we shall have the assistance of all our Allies. I hope that Russia will soon come into line, but the burden of this struggle for liberty will fall upon France, upon Great Britain and her daughter States, and upon the United States, and the characteristic policy of these great nations in defending civiliza tion and maintaining liberty is to be based upon conscription. When you have selective conscription, as the minister outlined it to-day, you get rid	of
all recruiting and its inconveniences. Many of the most patriotic men in the country never could quite see the reason why they should go out and tell the young men why they should go to the front. The law of conscription is based on the duty of each man to defend'the country and to protect the rights of his fellowmen, and when you have that law you do not need to exercise persuasion or ask a man to go as a matter of reason. Many a man says: tell me it is my duty by law and 1 will go. That reply has often been met in recruiting campaigns. The Government should do what they have done in England-and it will require a great deal of work on the part of the ginger party to get it through. The United States came to it, not because they were more active than any one else, but because they had the experience of the Mother Country. We have the experience of tooth now, and it is the duty of a united Parliament to pass a law of conscription, selective conscription if you like, but, in any case,* a law that will impose a duty upon the men of Canada. Probably the youngest men, those, say, of 21, could first be told that they must go to the war. The school boys will grow up under a system which tells them that it is the duty of those who are over 20 and 21 to go in the first draft, and that if more are required those who are older will be called upon. I am sure that when they know it is their duty there will be no objection. I do not care in which province they may live.

To my mind the only way to win the war is by adopting a vigorous policy of conscription. I hope that a measure to this end will toe introduced into Parliament right away, and that it will be passed. I believe that the men will go gladly and that there will then be no trouble in filling up the ranks of the battalions we have there now. And we need more; as was pointed out this afternoon, those who are over there are calling to us to give them
assistance,	and	we have to	heed	thatcall.	This	Parliament, then,	will	notbe	doing	its	duty unless	it	enacts	a law of	conscription	and	then
enforces it. The result will be our ability to increase the number of our soldiers overseas by 100,000, or if necessary, 200,000 men and, carried out on the selective principle, the law will result in no man being sent forward who is more useful here in the munitions plants, as a grain grower, as a farmer, as a railroad man or as one who is engaged in anything essential to the ordinary life of the community. We have that principle recognized at last. I do not know what stand hon. gentlemen opposite will take in regard to it. But a good many of their supporters in my province, pronounced Liberals, are declaring every day that they want to see conscription in Canada. We have to have it to win the war. Now that the ball has been set rolling, the ginger policy-

maintopic: THE PRIME MINISTER'S VISIT TO ENGLAND.
speechtext: What will they say now?

maintopic: THE PRIME MINISTER'S VISIT TO ENGLAND.
speechtext:
Thousands of
them are saying that they are in favour of conscription. I do not think all the loyalty is on the side of one party in this country; I would not want to live in Canada if that were the case. Anyway, you want to give every man an opportunity of saying whether he accepts the law-and it is the first law of any community that every citizen ought to be willing to defend its liberties. Some people have left our country because they feared conscription on the other side of the line. But that is one of the accidents of a condition of war; it is a common trait of humanity. I believe that Canadians irrespective of politics will support conscription just as the Britishers in the old land, irrespective of politics, supported it there. Among the most useful things they have in Great Britain in connection with the militia are the courts of tribunals which mobilize the men, size them up and find out those who are fit to

go to the war and those who are necessary in munitions plants, the farming industry or other essential occupations. In that way the air is cleared-and that is the great thing, to clarify the situation with regard to the war. You clarify the situation with regard to the prosecution of the war through the adoption of conscription as you could do in no other way.
Conscription has been found to he absolutely essential in Great Britain and France; the United States have just declared themselves to be in favour of it, and now that we have taken the same attitude, there is a much brighter prospect of winning the war. We are engaged in a struggle against an organization of nations which depend absolutely on conscription for their war efforts. If, as the Prime Minister said this afternoon, Germany has brought into her armies a million men more than she had a year ago, that has been accomplished by reason of the law of conscription in force in that country. In a struggle against conscription as it exists in Germany, you cannot overcome Germany nor defend civilization, nor maintain the liberty of the world unless you fight the devil with fire, if conscription is the fire he uses against you. That view came home long ago to the boys who are giving their services at the front and many of whom have made the supreme sacrifice. It is going to come home to this House and to the people of this country. It is the view taken by the women of this country; it is the view taken by many a Canadian mother whose boy has been killed on the battlefield and who cannot understand why some other mother's boy should not take his place in the field, if the struggle is for the liberties, not only for this country, but of the world. I absolutely agree with what the Prime Minister and the leader of the Opposition have said this afternoon, namely, that this war must be won, and, if it is to be won, it can be won only by the adoption of the principle of conscription. And when we adopt that one principle of the ginger party in Great Britain, we shall have to adopt their principles in relation to other matters I have spoken about this evening. I wish, therefore, to congratulate the Government on at last adopting this policy. The Government have taken a good while to adopt it, and some reconstruction of the Government and more unity in this Parliament may be required to carry it into effect. I am, however, prepared to face any change that will give us a more vigorous policy,
not only in regard to conscription, but in regard to everything necessary to win the war. The other question as to what our relations are to be between the component parts of the Empire need not concern us now; that will take care of itself after the war. The Prime Minister in the British House of Commons said yesterday, and it was 'also told us here this afternoon that the question would be discussed later on; but the question of the rela-9 p.m. tions between the component parts of the Empire is not the question before us to-day. The question at issue is the winning of the war. We may as well recognize the fact that conscription is necessary for the winning of the war; that question faces us now, and I hope that the Government will not delay in bringing down their proposals in regard to conscription and that the House will not delay in carrying them into effect.

maintopic: THE PRIME MINISTER'S VISIT TO ENGLAND.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend made the suggestion that there ought to be more ginger in the Government. This reminds me of the fact that some years ago a horse dealer in St. John had a horse to sell, and he loaded him up with ginger, and as the horse appeared lively and in fine condition he wias able to sell the animal, but after the effects of the ginger wore away the horse was the same old horse.

maintopic: THE PRIME MINISTER'S VISIT TO ENGLAND.
speechtext:
Will my hon. friend say that Lloyd George is only a ginger horse?
-Mr. PUGSLEY: This occasion gives me an opportunity of speaking concerning a subject which is very dear to my heart, and which has been suggested by my right hon. friend the leader of the Government. I refer to the subject of shipbuilding in Canada. The Prime Minister stated that the great cry of Lloyd George was for ships, more ships, still more ships. Those in this country who have given the subject any consideration whatever lare not surprised that the demand should have arisen for more ships. That demand has been increasing ever since this war broke out. Any man with any foresight, any man whose duty it has been to look ahead to the interest of this country must have foreseen that the time would come when ships would be imperatively required in order to carry on the transportation business, not only of Canada so far as its coastal transportation is concerned, but between Canada and the Mother Country. Yet, to-day we are in this lamentable position, that-to

post of duty where their presence was required. One very important subject that came up for the consideration of those jingoists in England, who have a certain amount of influence with the present Government, and whose representative is, I think, a former citizen of Canada, Lord Beaver-brook, who himself advocated the scheme, and who, I have no doubt, had a great deal to do with these hon. gentlemen being invited to go to England at this time,, was the reconstruction of the Empire, the question of Imperial federation. We know that there are a good many people in England who have been strongly agitating that question, and have been hoping that the Dominion would be drawn into an arrangement of that kind. But I believe that if that arrangement were consummated it would ' be the first step toward the breaking up of the Empire, instead of a step toward its greater consolidation. The Prime Minister tells us that that question was considered. He expressed his great thanks to the group of young enthusiasts in Great Britain who had been so earnestly agitating Imperial federation. But the Conference passed1 a resolution identical with the position taken by Sir Wilfrid Laurier when he attended the Imperial Conferences. I have here extracts from one of the leading English newspapers making reference to the speech of General Smuts. I think the people have a great deal to thank General Smuts for; I. believe that he, moire than all others, has prevented the idea of Imperial federation going into effect so far as the Conference was concerned. Here is what is reported in the Ottawa Journal of this evening, in a telegram from London.:
London, May 18.-Editorially discussing General Smuts' speech, in which he regarded the British Empire not as a state, but as a system of nations, the Daily Telegraph says it is a difference which goes to the very root of the Imperial fabric. "The oneness of New Zealand or Australia with Great Britain," says the Telegraph, "must he different not merely from that of India, where there is no kinship of blood or community of language and ideas, but also from that of Canada and South Africa, in each of which are two sturdy different stocks which, at the present time, can hardly be said to desire complete fusion, even as an ideal.
'To ignore this great fact because it is an awkward stumbling block to the realization of a cherished political theory is not statesmanship, but the negation of statesmanship.''
Referring to General Smuts' assertion, that the British commonwealth of nations does not stand for standardization or conventionalism, the Telegraph says:	'There is one other
great Imperial statesman who will certainly applaud and endorse that sentiment, namely, Sir Wilfrid Laurier. It is exactly the point

he has always laid stress on when Imperial federationists have seemed to him to press forward at too rapid a pace."
That is a striking tribute to the stand that Sir Wilfrid Laurier took during all the years he was at the head of the Government of Canada. The final action of this War Cabinet is the greatest possible Tebuke to those who have been condemning Sir Wilfrid Laurier because he has always pronounced for the autonomy of Canada and other overseas dominions of the Empire. Then, again, what a striking endorsement it is of the position which the Liberal party has always taken in reference to the British preference. After many days of conference the Imperial War Cabinet came to the conclusion that the British Parliament should not impose any duty on foodstuffs, and that the overseas dominions did not expect Britain to give any preference upon foodstuffs* coming from those dominions. But there was no need to go to London to have that declared. That was declared, so far as Canada was concerned, in 1897, when the British preference was established by the Parliament of Canada, at the instance of the Liberal party led by Sir Wilfrid Laurier. At that time the Liberal Government and the Parliament of Canada said to the British people: We give you a preference in the markets of this country for all the manufactures and other products of Great Britain; we give you that preference freely and voluntarily, exacting nothing in return; we do not ask the Imperial Parliament to tax foodstuffs and to make dearer the food of the British people. It would be interesting for you, Mr. Speaker (Mr. Blain) to look over the pages of Hansard and see how the party led by the present Prime Minister regarded that action of the Liberal party at that time. They condemned that action. They said it was entirely against the interests of Canada to grant any preference in Canada unless the Imperial Parliament also granted a preference to the foodstuffs of Canada in the markets of Great Britain. And, if I am not mistaken, it is on record that the right hon. gentleman (Sir Robert Borden) voted against a resolution in this Parliament approving the action of the Government of that day in granting the British preference. I know his party voted in that way, and i think hi3 name is recorded with the others. There was no occasion for three members of the Government to go to England for the purpose of having that declared a proper policy, which was declared twenty years ago by this Parliament and approved of generally by the people of Britain.

If you eliminate these matters to which I have referred, what else is there of importance that the Imperial War Cabinet considered? They considered the question of the temptations placed in the way of our soldiers at the front. Sir George Per-ley is the acting High Commissioner for Canada, and Overseas Minister, receiving a very handsome salary. One would suppose that he could acquaint this Government with what is going on and that through him any action reasonably possible to take might be taken. This, surely, was not a subject making necessary investigation by these gentlemen for so many weeks, if not months. I can not at the moment think of anything else of urgent importance that was considered. The Prime Minister says that he has noticed in the papers suggestions that he and his colleagues were having a good time in England. We can not be blamed for what the newspapers say, and I am inclined to think that the newspapers can not be blamed for the reports they give. It was open to every one to see, day after day and week after week, what was going on. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen) the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) and the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers), we read, dined with His Majesty the King. The newspapers could not blind their eyes to the fact that the Prime Minister received the freedom of several cities in England, and that excellent speeches were made on these occasions. The newspapers must have seen that these gentlemen, during the Easter holidays and at other times, were having a good time-

maintopic: THE PRIME MINISTER'S VISIT TO ENGLAND.
speechtext: Surely the hon. gentleman does not call that of which he has just been speaking "having a good time"?

maintopic: THE PRIME MINISTER'S VISIT TO ENGLAND.
speechtext:
A very excellent and pleasant time. But, as to real work, I would like these gentlemen to tell us what they have done that could not have been done equally well by correspondence or through the Overseas Minister, who is also the acting High Commissioner? When they went to England, I joined heartily with other members on this side of the House in wishing them Godspeed on their journey, and in expressing the hope that they would be able to accomplish something for Canada and for the Empire. They come back empty handed except with this beautiful mace that is now lying on the Table. My right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition was happy in the Temarks which he made in reference to that a few days ago. Really that is the only tangible, the only substantial thing that they have brought back.
But just a word in regard to the very important subject which my right hon. friend has referred to and which, of course, has nothing to do with hie visit to the other side of the water. That is the question of conscription. This House, I would suppose, would hardly be called upon to express an opinion on this important question until the particulars have been brought down. The statement has been made that it is to be selective conscription. As to whether the country will be satisfied with the measure of conscription which is proposed will depend very much upon how the selection is to be made. I could understand that in England, where they have a national Government, a Government free from all partisanship, a Government whiifh is absolutely non-partisan ini its character, selective conscription could be worked out to the general satisfaction of the people. But if, in this country, when the war broke out, this Government had created an absolutely national, non-partisan Government, and if the war had been carried on irrespective of party consideration and of party patronage, the Government would be in a very different position to-day to ask the country to trust them with the duty of carrying out selective conscription. We have no intimation from the Prime Minister as to how the duty of carrying out the selection is to be performed. If patronage is to enter into it, if partisanship is to enter into it, as it appears to have entered into everything connected with the war, then it is very doubtful if the people of the country will be satisfied with it. I agree with my right hon. friend the leader of the Oposition that the people are united in their desire to do everything that is possible to win this war. If conscription is necessary in order to have more men available at the front, I think the people will agree to conscription, but I also think, Sir, that the people will demand that there shall be conscription, not merely of man power, but of the accumulated wealth in this country as well. They will demand that. The people, and especially the labouring people, will not be content that the youth of Canada should be conscripted and sent by force to the front while the wealth of this country is allowed to go scot free. It will demand that conscription shall be applied so as to do equal justice to all classes in the community. I shall await

with interest the 'bringing down of the measure providing for conscription before venturing any opinion, as to whether it should be approved of by the House, but I, as one humble member of this House would say that a great deal will depend on the mode in which selective-because that word "selective" is a most important word in connection with it-conscription is to be carried out.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. D. HAZEN (Minister of Marine and of Naval Service):
speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: THE PRIME MINISTER'S VISIT TO ENGLAND.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it will be admitted by every member of this House and by every person throughout the country wherever the speech of my right hon. friend is read, that this afternoon, dealing with a question of very great and far-reaching importance, that the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) made a deliverance that can be characterized properly and truthfully as dignified and statesmanlike. I think it may also be .said that my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfred Laurier), in his-short address, dealt with the matter in a way that was worthy of one occupying the high position he occupies in this House. The hon. member for South York (Sir. Maclean), who also addressed the House, spoke from the standpoint of the public interest, and it remained for my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley) to deal with this transcendent Imperial question from the standpoint of petty party politics.	It is to be regretted that
an hon. gentleman possessing the ability and long parliamentary experience of my hon. friend should never be able to get away, in dealing with any question before this House, from a desire to secure party advantage. As a matter of fact, the hon. gentleman of late years has got so that he cannot deal with any question, I think I am within the mark in saying so, from the standpoint of the public interest no matter how important that question may be to the people of the country, but he thinks it necessary, with every question, great or small, to descend into the realm of petty, partisan discussion irrespective of what the public interest may be, his desire being to advance party interests first and the interest of the country afterwards. I think it is related of Queen Mary of England that she said that when she died the word " Calais " would be found engraved upon her heart. I am disposed to think that my hon. friend has taken Courtenay Bay so much to heart that when my hon. friend dies " Courtenay Bay " will be found en-
graved on his heart although, for personal reasons, I hope and trust that his demise may be postponed for a very long period. My hon. friend invariably, since the session of 1912, has repeated his speech on Courtenay Bay six or seven times during every session, and when he makes that speech I am always reminded of the story of the man who, to save time, instead of saying his prayers at night, had his prayer written on a card which he hung on a post at the foot of his bed, and when he got into bed he pointed to the card and said: Lord, those are my sentiments. It would save a great deal of the time of this House if the hon. gentleman would adopt some such course in regard to that speech which, I venture to say, nearly every hon. member of this House has by memory now and could get up and repeat in exactly the same words as my hon. friend has used here tonight and on many previous occasions. I must say, however, that there are some very notable omissions from the speech of my hon. friend. My hon. friend always puts it forward that had the contract been awarded for cruisers and destroyers, for which tenders were asked by the Government of which he was a member, they would have been built at Courtenay Bay in the vicinity of St. John. My hon. friend always forgets to tell this House, what I must remind him. of, how these tenders were received nearly six months before the date of the general election of 1911, and how they were placed in a pigeon hole in one of the departments and never again saw the light of day. If the hon. gentleman had been in earnest, if he had been sincere, if he had ever believed that they were to be built in Courtenay Bay, would he have allowed six months, or practically six months, to pass without any action being taken upon them? When the hon. gentleman went out of power the tenders were resurrected from the pigeon hole to which they had been consigned. My hon. friend says that these vessels would have been built at Courtenay Bay. My hon. friend always forgets to tell this House that his honoured leader told this House that had his Government stayed in power these cruisers and destroyers would have been built at Montreal.
I have previously asked my hon. friend to reconcile the statement he so often makes with the statement of his leader, but that he has not been able to do and cannot do. For six months those tenders weTe pigeonholed and northing was done; but when the elections took place It was held out as a glittering bait to the people of St. John,

the people of Halifax, the people of Montreal, and the people of Sydney that if the Government was returned to power theirs would be the places where those cruisers and destroyers would be built. When I came into office as Minister of the Naval Service I found'-

maintopic: THE PRIME MINISTER'S VISIT TO ENGLAND.
speechtext:
I wish to correct my
hon. friend. My hon. friend says that for six months these tenders remained in a pigeon hole. I want to tell (him that these tenders and specifications were taken by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to England for the purpose of consultation with the authorities there, and brought back from England very shortly before the elections took place.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: THE PRIME MINISTER'S VISIT TO ENGLAND.
speechtext: And that is the explanation my hon. friend made to this House before, an explanation that must be utterly unsatisfactory .to this House and to the people of this country. Why were they taken to England? Why were they not dealt with here? To-night my hon. friend objects because members of the Government went to England at the request of the British Government. Why should this matter, a matter that should have been dealt with by the Government of Canada if they had madte up their minds as to the policy they were to pursue, why, may I ask my hon. friend, who talks so much about Canadian autonomy to-night, should these tenders be taken to England? Parliamentary language might perhaps not permit me to say-

maintopic: THE PRIME MINISTER'S VISIT TO ENGLAND.
speechtext: Does the minister want my answer?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: THE PRIME MINISTER'S VISIT TO ENGLAND.
speechtext: -that the excuse is a mere excuse and is not a reason.

maintopic: THE PRIME MINISTER'S VISIT TO ENGLAND.
speechtext: Will the minister allow me to answer, or does he desire an answer?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: THE PRIME MINISTER'S VISIT TO ENGLAND.
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman waits until I have concluded my speech he may answer. The hon. gentleman has a habit of always interrupting when a member is addressing the House-

maintopic: THE PRIME MINISTER'S VISIT TO ENGLAND.
speechtext: You asked me a question

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: THE PRIME MINISTER'S VISIT TO ENGLAND.
speechtext:
And while that is the case there is no member so sensitive to interruption or who resents it so much as my hon. friend when he is on his feet. I say that my hon. friend when again addressing the House on this subject would do well to tell the facts of the case. It makes little difference, they have been told over and over
again in this country and are well known to the people. My hon. friend can go on repeating his excuse for many years to come but he will fail to make any impression upon the people of Canada or on the people of the constituency which he especially desires to influence by the statements he is making in regard to this matter.
My hon friend (Mr. Pugsley) has to-night made the claim that this Government has done nothing to advance ship building in Canada. One would think from the statement of my hon. friend that really nothing was being done about the building of ships in this country. Let me point out, what every member knows, that every ship yard in Canada is full to capacity at the present time, building ships for the purposes of the British Government and for purposes of trade between this country and Great Britain. My hon. friend says that the Imperial Munitions Board will not award contracts for ships of less than 2,500 tons. Let us see what has been the connection of the Imperial Munitions Board, a Board responsible to the British Government alone, with this matter. The British Government, after the reconstruction of the Cabinet under the leadership of Mr. Lloyd George, appointed a controller of shipping, and for that position they obtained the services of one of the most experienced shipping men in the world, Sir Joseph MacLay, the head of a great shipping firm in the city of Glasgow, a firm known the world over. Sir Joseph MacLay has been wrestling with this question of acquiring ships since he came into office; it is admitted on all sides in the British Isles that no more capable man could be found for the task. When I was in Great Britain I spent many hours with Sir Joseph MacLay and his officers discussing these matters. I was at his office time after time, discussing with him and members of the Department over which he presides, the shipping situation, pointing out to them the advantages which were offered in Canada for the conetruction. of ships, and I do not think I am speaking in any language of exaggeration when I say that I believe it was in part at least due to the efforts I made that many of those contracts upon which our Canadian ship yards are now working were placed in Canada. These ships are being built for Great Britain and for British trade. They are being built for the purpose of relieving, as far as may be, the serious condition of affairs that exists



to-day, because, in consequence of the operations of the submarines, and of the fact that Great Britain has had to supply shipping not only to meet the requirements and wants of the people of the British Isles, but also the requirements of her Allies, there has not been available as much shipping ias is necessary to carry to Great Britain the commodities required for use there. As a result of that situation, the greatest economy and frugality must be exercised, and that condition will continue to exist between now and the next harvest, in order that the people of the British Isles may have sufficient food for their wants. As a matter of fact, the condition is so serious that for three or four weeks before we left Great Britain no potatoes at all were served at the hotel where we were staying, or at any hotel in the city of London. Sugar was extremely scarce, and flour was scarce and had to be carefully husbanded. At the hotel where we were staying, under the order of the director of food supply, Lord Devonport, only a small portion of bread was .served to the guests at each meal, and we saw no such thing as white bread, because the wheat flour was being mixed with rye and with meal made from barley in order to make the wheat flour go as far as possible. That is the state of affairs, and it has been brought about in consequence of the lack of tonnage to carry foodstuffs in large quantities to feed the people of the British Isles.

maintopic: THE PRIME MINISTER'S VISIT TO ENGLAND.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: THE PRIME MINISTER'S VISIT TO ENGLAND.
speechtext:
I do not think for a moment that there is going to be starvation in the British Isles. There is lots of food of certain sorts. There seemea to be no lack of meat or fish or other foods of that sort. Still, economy and frugality and prudence will have to be exercised, and Sir Joseph MacLay is doing his utmost, with a large staff of competent shipping men about him, to utilize the shipping facilities of Great Britain, Canada and all other parts of the world. In order to make good as far as possible the ravages , and losses caused by the submarine campaign and by the diver-serion of a large number of ships from commercial traffic in consequence of their being employed in the transport of troops and munitions to distant countries and theatres of war, these steps are necessary.
All these facts are in the mind of the shipping controller, who occupies a most responsible position to-day. In consequence of that, he is making arrangements for the building of ships in Canada, through the
[Mr Hazen.]
instrumentality of the Imperial Munitions Board, which is responsible to the British Government alone, the expenses' being financed I believe, although I am not quite positive, in whole by the Government of Canada, who are making the advances for the purpose of carrying on this work. However, I make this statement subject to correction, because certain arrangements were made when I was away and I have not been able to catch up with my work since my return and get full information on all the subjects with which I should be familiar. As I say, those contracts are being made in Canada, but the shipping controller and his staff have decided that the ships they require are to be of not less than 2,500 tons dead weight capacity.
That is the decision that the British Government has come to through the responsible department of the shipping controller. It is for that reason that the Imperial Munitions Board cannot place contracts for ships that are smaller than 2,500 tons. There is no doubt that in different parts of Canada, along the coast of the Maritime Provinces, in British Columbia, on the St. Lawrence and at other places, many ships can toe built and are being built to-day. In the province of Nova Scotia a large number of ships

maintopic: THE PRIME MINISTER'S VISIT TO ENGLAND.
speechtext: By private parties.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: THE PRIME MINISTER'S VISIT TO ENGLAND.
speechtext:
By private parties, and
these private parties, at the present rate of freight, if they have any luck at all and escape the submarines, will make most handsome dividends and profits. Numbers of ships are being built to-day by private parties. '

maintopic: THE PRIME MINISTER'S VISIT TO ENGLAND.
speechtext: Could the minister tell me the highest tonnage of these ships?

maintopic: THE PRIME MINISTER'S VISIT TO ENGLAND.
speechtext:
I am told that the ships
being built in Nova Scotia run from 1,500 tons down to small vessels of say 150 ipns. I believe that a large number of them are under construction in Nova Scotia. When I was in England I pointed out to the Shipping Controller the desirability of utilizing all the wopden shipping possible foT the purpose of carrying foods across the ocean. Since Tet/urning to Canada I have again communicated with Sir Joseph Maclay and Right Hon. Walter Long, impressing the desirability of the matter upon them and asking for further consideration of it.

maintopic: THE PRIME MINISTER'S VISIT TO ENGLAND.
speechtext: Why do they not accept smaller vessels?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: THE PRIME MINISTER'S VISIT TO ENGLAND.
speechtext:
What ground of criticism is there against the Government because the Imperial Munitions Board is not awarding contracts for the construction of ships of less than 2,500 tpns, having regard to the statement of facts that 'I have put before the House to-night? In what way is the Canadian Government responsible or tjo blame for that? After all, if we have shipyards employed to their utmost capacity; if smaller yards are employed by private individuals who aTe enterprising enough to go into business and to build ships in very considerable numbers, in what way does the interest of the country suffer? though at the same time I would hope that the British Government would see its way clear as a matter of policy to decide that ships of less than 2,500 tons should be built for them in Canada under the control and jurisdiction of the Munitions Board. When my hon. friend addressed the House he should have known, if he did not know, that in wliat they were doing the Imperial Munitions Board were following the direction of the Shipping Controller of Great Britain. If he did know that, or if he did not know it-more especially if he did know it-it is evident that my hon. friend was not so desirous of assisting to advance the commercial and shipbuilding interests of Canada as he was to score a point against the Government, basing his argument on premises that were not substantial and on a condition of affairs for which the Government are in no sense responsible. These are the facts, and that is my excuse for replying to what my hon. friend said this afternoon.
Passing from what my hon. friend has said, I would refer for a few moments to the remarks that were made this afternoon by the right hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition, My right hon. friend had very little criticism to make with regard to the statement of the right hon. leader of the House as to what occurred at the meetings of the Imperial War Cabinet and of the Imperial Conference. My hon. friend did indulge in a little criticism of the hon. Prime Minister because the Minister of Public Works wias one of the gentlemen who were asked to accompany him to England. The right hon. leader of the Opposition said that in his opinion the two ministers who should have accompanied him to England were the Minister of Naval Service and the Minister of Militia. The Minister of Militia declined to go to England because he had been in office only a
99 J
few weeks, was overburdened with work, had upon his shoulders the responsibility of what is to-day the most important department of the Government, and had to acquire a knowledge of that department to enable him to administer it with the success with which, I am glad to say, he is administering it. Moreover, there is an Overseas Minister of Militia in the person, of Sir George Perley, a very capable business man who is devoting himeelf entirely to the work of the militia and of the High Commissioner's office in London. Having all these facts in mind, it was considered that it would be possible to allow the Minister of Militia to remain in his office at Ottawa and that the hon. Minister of Public Works might accompany the Prime Minister in his place to the old country. When there we were in constant and daily touch with Sir George Perley; we were in constant and daily touch with the authorities in the War Office, and with the authorities of the Admiralty Department. The right hon. gentleman,, in making this criticism, did not press the point very much and was not himself, I believe, very strongly impressed with the force of the criticism that he was making.
The member for St. John says that the Conference and the War Cabinet were barren of result and he would have the country 'believe that the members of the Government who were over there were not engaged in serious work; that they were, indulging in junketing trips about the country; that they were simply enjoying themselves in a social way and were not properly attending to the business of the country. I eay, Sir, that a meaner insinuation was never made to this Parliament or to the people. In many respects I entertain a feeling of great regard for my hon. friend, but I say that it is not worthy of him to make a charge of that kind against the Prime Minister and two of the members of the Government. Not only is it unworthy of him, but it is another evidence of the fact that he views the questions that come before this House only from the narrow standpoint of petty politics and that he cannot rise to the position of a statesman and discuss big issues in a statesmanlike, dignified and proper manner as is fitting in a great Parliament like this. Let me tell my hon. friend that while I am in Ottawa during the session of the House, every moment of my time is occupied. Any man who has been in a ministerial position, as many of my hon. friends whom I see opposite have been, know that no man can discharge the duties

of a minister of the Crown during a session of Parliament in ordinary times, without devoting his whole thought, time and attention to the duties of that office. But busy as I have been during the past sessions, more especially since the war broke out, and during the time when extraordinary work has been thrown uipon the department of which I am the head, I never did a greater amount of harder and more exacting work during a session of Parliament in Ottawa than I had to perform during the time I was in Great Britain. It was a relief to me when we got on the steamer at Liverpool on our way to Canada to obtain a few days rest after the strenuous work that we had beeen undertaking.
I am sure my hon. friend will realize how unfair it is that the suggestion should go -abroad that men in responsible positions in the Government, when upon a mission which in point of importance was as great -as any that Canadian statesmen ever went [DOT]on, should be idling away their time, indulging in social pleasures and neglecting the business for which they went overseas.
My hon. friend is not satisfied with what the Imperial Conference has done; nor is he satisfied with what the War Cabinet has done. In this respect, my hon. friend differs very much from the gentleman who at the present time, with the general consent of all parties in the state, is Prime Minister of Great Britain. Mr. Lloyd George, in addressing the War Cabinet at its last meeting, gave us .this message. Let me remind the House, however, in the first place, that three days in the week we had meetings of the Imperial Conference and, on the other three days, meetings of the Imperial War Cabinet. Im addition to that there were committees on which we served, and it was my privilege to serve on two or three most important committees, one, regarding tonnage restrictions, on which I served along with members of the British Government and members of the Overseas Governments, another with regard to conditions which might arise when terms of peace were proposed, and on this latter committee there were four members of the British Cabinet and it was presided oveT by Lord Curzon, who himself was one of the five members of the British WaT Cabinet. Mr. Lloyd George, in saying farewell to us, said that the presence of the overseas representatives of the War Cabinet not only was an encouragement and a support to the Government of Great Britain, but had [ 'Mr Hazen.]
proved to them a real .and genuine help. He further said that everything that the British Government knew had been unreservedly placed at the . disposal of the representatives of the overseas Dominions, and that it would be .a great mistake if the experiment that had been made in calling together an Imperial War Cabinet this year was not repeated and incorporated in the very machinery of the Empire. That, he said, was the opinion of every member of the British Government. For that reason Mr. Lloyd George said that in his opinion, war or no war, a session of the Imperial War Cabinet should be convened at least annually, for the purpose of reviewing, apart from the waT, the general foreign, policy of the British Empire. It was inconceivable, he said that after this war, the overseas Dominions should not be, not only fully informed as to .all matters of foreign policy, but consulted before any such policy was agreed upon by the British Government, and he went on then to. say that in his opinion, as the Prime Minister stated this afternjon, the Imperial Cabinet should consist of the Prime Minister of Great Britain and certain other ministers, such as the Colonial Secretary, the Secretary of State for India, the War Minister and the First Lord of the Admiralty, whose duties would naturally bring them more closely in touch with Imperial affairs than others, and the Prime Ministers of the overseas Dominions. He did not refer to the overseas Dominions as dependencies, as I was sorry to hear my hon. friend on the other .side refer to them to-night. The word "dependency" grates harshly on my ear. Mr. Lloyd George said that the Prime Ministers of the overseas Dominions should attend these War Conferences, and if the Prime Minister of any overseas Dominion was for any reason unable to attend, then a minister delegated by him and given extensive powers should attend and also such other ministers from the overseas Dominions as the Prime Minister considered would be of value at the conference, because of any information they might through their departments possess of matters of special import concerning the Dominions overseas and the relations of the Empire abroad. That was the opinion of Mr. Lloyd George, and he said that that was the opinion of every member of the Government. The Government of Great Britain to-day is composed of men of different political faiths. There axe men who are Liberals, men who are Conservatives and men who are special

representatives of the great labour interests of the country. The War Cabinet, for instance, consists of five men: Mr. Lloyd George, a Liberal; Mr. Bonar Law, a Conservative; Lord Milner and Lord Curzon, Conservatives, and Mr. Arthu: Henderson, the representative of the labour interests of the countrv. The Government itself, outside of the War Cabinet, is composed of men of different political par-
10 p.m. ties, and Mr. Lloyd George, speaking for them, referred to the services rendered by the overseas representatives at the War Cabinet in the language which I have used, and which is substantially correct, even, I think in many cases, to the words that he used. That being the case, perhaps those of us who accompanied the Prime Minister overseas and the Prime Minister himself will not feel so badly, as we otherwise might at the fact that the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) thinks we are of no service and have accomplished no good.
Something has been said to-night about Imperial federation. I never knew exactly what was meant by Imperial federation, except this: there never was any hard or fast scheme to which any great body of people in this country committed themselves, and my understanding of the phrase Imperial federation did not necessarily imply an Imperial Parliament; it did not necessarily imply the sacrifice of a single iota of our autonomy or independence or liberty. If it did no man in this country would support such an idea for a single moment. What I have always understood by Imperial federation was that there should be a closer drawing together in the bonds of union, friendship, sympathy and common support, and the maintenance of a common Empire of Great Britain and its overseas Dominions and India and all the countries generally that make up the British Empire. Speaking from that standpoint,-I believe that the result flowing from that meeting of the War Cabinet this year, with the declaration that no question of foreign policy will be embarked upon without the overseas Dominions being consulted and without all the information being placed before them, is the greatest advance in the way of linking together more closely for common support and for the objects that are dear to the hearts of the people throughout the Empire that has occurred since the British Empire was first known to exist. To-day we have the fact that on an equal footing, with Great Britain, perhaps, being primus inter pares-the first among equals
-our statesmen, whatever party may be in power, are to meet year by year with the members of the British Cabinet for the purpose of considering and discussing questions that are for the interest and promotion of the cause of Empire the world over. Could there have been taken any more effective step without sacrificing one single jot or iota of our independence, political freedom or political autonomy? I believe, when party passion disappears, and the events of this year are viewed dispassionately, as they will be by the historian of the future, it will be admitted that one of the greatest steps ever taken for the advancement of the cause of this Empire and the uniting together more closely its component parts in bonds of friendship that in no way interfere with the independence of the Empire, was taken during the last few weeks, and it is one that I believe will, in the future, redound to the advancement of every part of this Empire and go a long way towards ensuring the future peace of the world. I did not intend ito speak tonight, and I do not want to trespass much upon the time of the House, because there may be another opportunity for taking up. in detail the questions that have been referred to. The resolutions that were passed at the Conference I do not intend to take up in detail, nor at any great length, but there are a few matters that have been referred to in the course of the debate this afternoon in regard to which I will crave a few moments of the indulgence of the House before I take my seat.
Reference was made in this House and we saw references in the press to the drinking habits of the Canadian soldiers in the different camps in which they were placed in Great Britain. I want to tell this House in regard to that matter a few facts, more in detail than the matter was referred to by the Prime Minister this afternoon. At one of the meetings of the Imperial Conference Sir Edward Henry, Chief of Police of the city of London, appeared before us, and he told us that in what he spoke of as the London area, there were from three to four hundred thousand soldiers every night; that many of them were on leave from the trenches, and many of them were going to or coming from the front. As a result, the streets of London were frequented in large numbers by these men.
Most of them were men without relatives or friends, and many of them naturally sought human society and human comfort, and yet Sir Edward Henry told us that of the 300,000 or 400,000 men who were in the

London area every night, the largest number of soldiers who bad ever been arrested in one night for drunkenness was 16, and the number hardly ever exceeded 10 or 13. I do not think anything could speak more strongly for the sobriety and good-behavior of the soldiers there. The soldiers Sir Henry referred to were not all Canadians; some were from Australia, or New Zealand; many of them were British; and there were others from almost every quarter of the globe. These figures, I repeat, are a splendid tribute to the sobriety of the soldiers who are fighting the battles of the Empire at the present time.
Coming more directly to the Canadian soldier, against whom I understand a charge was made in this House, the day before I left England I received a letter from General Steele, in command of the Canadian troops at Shorncliffe. This letter was not written at any solicitation of mine.

One could not helip feeling impressed with the wonderful cheerfulness of the men at the front, their wonderful physique, and the wonderful work they are doing. I never met a man in the trenches who had a complaint to make about anything. They were trying to do their duty for the honour of the Empire and of Canada. And in the different hospitals I visited-and I visited many of them; whenever I had a spare hour or two I went to some of the various hospitals to inquire for our Canadian soldiers, and I think I must have talked to thousands of them -I found the same spirit of cheerfulness prevailing. As far as I could judge from my own observations and from the statements made to me by the men in [DOT]the hospitals, the Canadian hospital service is one that is a credit to the people of this country, and those whb have friends at the front should have the satisfaction of knowing 'that those friends will receive in our different hospitals the very best of treatment. All these hospitals are equipped with operating rooms, X-ray apparatus, and instruments as modern as can be found in the best hospitals in Canada. The best of Canadian surgeons and doctors are there, [DOT]and the best of Canadian nurses. And all over the land in England and France I found the women of Canada in the hospitals ministering to the wants of our soldiers who have unfortunately been wounded.
Let me tell a little story illustrating the (Spirit of the Canadian boys at the front. One night about ten o'clock, after I had returned from a visit to the military camp at Shoreham, I found a cable from a member of this House telling me that he had information that his son had been wounded, and asking me if I could ascertain where he was and what was his condition'. It was just after the battle of Vimy Ridge, and (many wounded were being brought across the Channel. I at once inquired by telephone among the different hospitals, and at length I found this young man was in the First London General Hospital, and the information I was given was that he had received- a flesh wound in 'the leg, that his condition was not serious, and that he was getting along very well. I wired this information to his father, and the next morning, being Sunday, I went to the hispital ito see him. And a 'more cheerful boy I [Mr Hazen.]
pever saw. Lying in the bed next to him was the brother of a member of this House, the hon. member for Centre York (Mr. Wallace), wounded, but I am glad to say, not seriously. And in another near-by bed was the Colonel of the regiment of the young man, the son of the hon. member for (Kingston (Mr. Nickle). He told me the iStory of the fight. Referring to my hon. friend's son, he said that early in the day the young man was wounded in the head' by a piece of shrapnel. The wound bled a good deal, and the young man was ordered back to a dressing station and to fall out. But he would mot do so; he said that he would be disgraced forever if he did; that he was there to help to 'take Yimy Ridge and he wanted to go on. His Colonel allowed him to have his way. Later in the fight, the boy received the wound which 'caused his removal [DOT]to the hospital. This is illustrative' of the courage and spirit that characterizes all our Canadian boys at the front, so far a3 I could see, without one single exception.
Many members of this House have sons in the fighting force. I think that nearly every member who has a son of military age has that son serving at the front. Some have unfortunately lost their eons in. the war The Prime Minister referred to the fact that arrangements had been made that the graveyards in which 'the Canadian soldiers are buried would 'be kept in proper condition in perpetuity at the expense of the British Government and the Governments of the overseas Dominions, through the agency of a commission of which the Prince of Wales is chairman. That, I have no doubt, is gratifying news to all the members of this House as it is gratifying to my-iself. When I was in France I visited a graveyard in which I have a very great personal interest. Lying side by side with ;my own dear boy I saw the names of other Canadians-of General Mercer; of the son of the late General Cotton; and the sons of other prominent Canadians-all sleeping their last sleep.. And extremely gratifying [DOT]it was to me to see the way in which that graveyard was kept and to observe the evidences that the loving hands of companions and comrades of these men who had given up their lives had done everything that could 'be done to brake their last resting place what their relatives and-friends overseas would desire to have it.
All through the Canadian forces, on every side, I found that feeling of comradeship, that feeling of affection one for another, that feeling of sacrifice and I felt, as I

looked over towards Vimy Ridge from Mount St. Eloi and was told that in a short time four Canadian divisions would be hurled against it, it would be little less than a crime if we in Canada did not see that these divisions were replenished, that all wastage was made good and that men would be kept going from Canada to sustain and strengthen the arms of those who had been fighting so valiantly for pur cause over there. Whilst at the outset of the war I thought that the effect of men voluntarily coming forward to serve their King and country without any compulsion at all was a much grander and more inspiring sight than would be that of men being brought forward under compulsion, I also made up my mind that if the voluntary system failed it would be our bounden duty as Canadians to adopt methods similar to those which have been adopted in practically every other country in the world and to see that men went forward from Canada to fill up the ranks of those who bad fallen in the fight and were incapacitated from further service. That is the reason that actuated me in giving my consent to a policy which might be described as compulsory service or conscription, or whatever you may choose to call it, such as was announced by my right hon friend the Prime Minister this afternoon, a policy which this Government intend to stand or fall by in the estimation of the people of this country.
There are many other matters that I might speak about in regard to our visit but I feel that it is unnecessary to do so; in fact at this late hour, time will hardly permit. There will be future opportunities of discussing perhaps more in detail some of the matters of interest to this country that we came in contact with on this trip abroad. Let me say, however, that grievously as we have been stricken by the war, great as is the sacrifice, personally, financially and commercially that the people of Canada have had to make, yet there is some satisfaction in knowing that wherever you go in France or England you find the praise of Canada, and what Canada has done, on the lips of every one. As a result pf what Canada has done, Canada's name to-day looms larger in the opinion of the world than ever it did before and it has taken a war to make the people understand the wonderful resources of Canada and the wonderful vigour of Canadians of the present generation.

glad that I made a reference to him because if I had not done sp it would not have given us the opportunity of listening to the very eloquent, interesting and affecting speech that the hon. gentleman has made. The minister .stated that every shipyard in Canada is occupied to-day. in building ships for the Imperial Munitions Board. I would like the minister to tell me what number of vessels are being built and where they are being built. 'There are a number of shipyards in the Maritime Provinces where wooden vessels were bpilt in the past, but where there are no ships being built now.

When I say that every shipyard is filled to its capacity I do not refer to shipyards which were shipyards in the past, but where no ship has been built for many years. I refer to shipyards where people have a plant and are ready to receive proposals for the construction of ships. I refer to Mr. Davies at Quebec, the Canadian Vickers Company at Montreal, the shipyards of Collingwood, the Poison Iron Works at Toronto, Couglan & Son on the Pacific coast, and the Wallace shipyards on the Pacific coast. I believe that ships are being built at the present time at New Glasgow by the Nova Scotia Steel Company. These are shipyards I had in my mind. There are places, for instance, along the St. John river, amongst them Oromocto, where I was born, at which ships have been built. At Oromocto there were three shipyards, buit no ship has been built in them for the last forty years. However, I will be very glad to get the information for my hon. friend.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a great deal of interest to the hon. Minister of Marine .and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen), and I suppose it is only fair as a member of this House that I should extend to him my congratulations upon the very excellent presentation of the case which he has placed before the House, and also my sympathy with 'him in the trying ordeal of visiting the ground on which his 'beloved son has shared the fate of many other Canadians who have given up their lives for the sacred cause and for their country. I have listened with a good deal of attention to the whole of my hon. friend's speech, and, going back to the first of it, where he accused my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley) of

making the same speech so often, I am not going to join issue upon the fact as to whether the hon. gentleman has made that speech often or not, as I can say to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries that, no matter how many times the hon. gentleman has made that speech, the same reply exactly has been made to it by the Minister of Marine .and Fisheries. If the short prayer " Those are my sentiments," applies to the one, it equally applies to the other. I am sure I do not find fault with the Minister of Marine for saying that the speech of the hon. member for St. John has been repeated quite a few times. It is a good speech; it is full of meat, and it is important to the people of St. John and of Courtenay Bay. He tells us that very likely the hon. member for St. John 'yill find the words "Courtenay Bay ." engraved upon his heart. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries had better take care that he will not find them engraved upon his political tombstone, because this is a very live issue in that part of the country, and the people may take care to point out that this was the finish of a man who had had a very happy career, but who fell at Courtenay Bay because he did not carry out schemes which were of great advantage to the people of the country and here he lies. The Minister of Marine gave us as the reason why they did not go on with shipbuilding in 1911 that the minister of that day thought it proper to consult the Admiralty. I think it was absolutely proper that he should consult the Admiralty in connection with the building of ships, and that the pattern that would be followed by shipbuilders of this cohntry should be as much as possible the same as that followed on the other side.
But I am very glad to be able to quote to the Minister of Marine an authority on that line of action that he will not dispute; that authority will be himself. When he spoke in this House for the first time after the last election, speaking in the same capacity and office in which he is to-day, on the 22nd of November, 1911, he expressed the position in which he and his Government were with regard to consulting the Admiralty. He said: I
I think the people of this country will approve of the action of this Government in hesitating before rushing hastily into a policy which must involve an expenditure of so many million dollars every year. I think they will appreciate the course of this Government in doing what was stated by the Prime Minister in his admirable speech in reply to the right hon. leader of the Opposition, when he said it was the intention of the Government to consider with the English Admiralty this whole

naval question from first to last. When we have done that, I think we will be able to come before this House and this country with a policy that will appeal to all Canadians as a policy that will be the best for the people of Canada and the best in the interest of the empire in which we live.
If it was wrong for the Minister of Pub-Works of the Government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier to propose consulting the Admiralty before launching upon a shipbuilding policy, was it right for the Government of the day? I think that it was quite proper in both Governments, but the hon. gentleman cannot now make any criticism against the former Government because we were consulting the Admiralty on this matter when that was also the policy of himself and of the Prime Minister under whom he holds office. I point this out to the minister in order that he may see that he is making a wrong line of criticism in adverting to the delay necessary to consult the Admiralty in the days of the Laurier Government and saying that'it was time ill spent and that there was no necessity for it. If the Laurier Government had continued in power they would have followed out the policy which they had enunciated and we would have had a navy of our. own; we would have been in the same proud position as Australia in defending not only her own waters but in extending defence to nearly all parts of the world where British interests are concerned. That is the isrtriking difference between the two policies. I would remind the Minister of Marine that the Government has been a long time in getting to work, that from the date of his address, the 22nd of November, 1911, until to-day, they have done nothing, although he then promised that the Government would in a short time bring down a policy that would be absolutely satisfactory to the people of this country, and carry it out.
The minister has been telling us that they worked very hard while they were away. While I was looking at the Minister of Marine and Fisheries and the Minister of Public Works and the Prime Minister yesterday and to-day, and when I heard their remarks about the food that was given to them in England, my mind reverted to the ancient days of the three Hebrew children, Shedrac, Meshac and Abednego, and I am glad indeed that the same result is present in the countenances of our children who went across. Those Hebrew children refused to partake of the fat things from the king's table; they would only take such ordinary food as pulse, etc. They thrived on it and looked fat and wholesome,

and I am glad to see our friends coming back in the same condition. But, after all,
I am disposed to think it was a nice holiday they had away, the long trips in the fresh air and the excellent good time which the Minister of Public Works knows so well how to enjoy and to suggest. I think it was rather that than the conduct of the Hebrew children that has brought them back looking so well; and if they are given to work on the other side of the Atlantic, my advice to the country generally would be to keep them there, because our experience with those three gentlemen, except the Prime Minister, is that they do not break their necks working, and if the Minister of Public Works was put to the task to show the great things that he has done since the war began, I am sure he would find some difficulty in pointing out anything conclusive or effective towards carrying on the war. I am sorry that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries is not here; if he were I would point out to him that all I know that he or his department did since the war began was to carry on reckless, partisan extravagance all along the coast from the western boundary of New Brunswick to the frozen zones of Labrador, in putting every little, miserable craft lying rotting on the shore before the war began into active service, and paying for them at the highest prices. I challenge, the minister or his department to place in the hands of members of the House a list of the boats, ships, scows and old tug boats that he has forced into the service of his department since the war began, and to tell the House and the country the owners of them, what they have cost the country and what they have been doing. If there is one scandalous thing in connection with this partisan war business from start to finish, it is that phase of the conduct of the department of the Minister of Marine. I intended to tell him that I do not blame him for it in any way, as he does not know; but his partisan agencies throughout the Maritime provinces know all about it, and if he will bring down the return I have suggested, the people of this country will know where millions of the money of this country is going. When we know that this is the extreme partisan way in which every phase of the war is carried forward, you will pardon us if we hesitate before we put the lives of our friends, under the rule of conscription, in the hands of hon. gentlemen opposite who have carried forward everything in connection with the
war strictly and absolutely along party lines. If conscription is to come, we trust that it will come in such a way that, we will not have the scandalous condition of things that officers will be sent through this country with the Tory brand, with the Tory heart, and the Tory intent, who will take away Grit boys and pass over the others by influences that certainly should not be brought to bear in this country. But when it is meeting us at every point, every turn of the road, in everything that they have touched in connection with this war, what hope have we that they will become rigliteous and high-minded all at once if this weapon of conscription is put in their hands? We can only judge their future by their past, and their past shows that there is nothing too strong, so far as party lines are concerned, to meet the approval and satisfaction of the members of this present Government.
My particular reason for replying to the Minister of Marine was to point out to him that the criticism he made in respect to shipbuilding and the delays that he alleges were committed and caused by the out-1 going Administration, were justified.
I think I should make one more comment in respect to the information that the minister gives us in connection with the criticism made on the wet canteen on the other side. I want to point out to the House and to you, Sir, when the word drunkenness is used, that is no evidence that there is insobriety. I wonder whether the minister ever heard the real definition of drunkenness. A man is drunk when he holds on to the grass for fear that he may fall backwards from the ground. A story is told of a man who was holding on to a telegraph post on the side of the road. He was asked what he was doing there, and he replied, "I am standing here until my old house comes around again." These are the conditions found in men who are drunk. Another story is told of a group of men who were drunk, one of whom called out to Mrs. Brown, whose head was out of the window: "Come down and pick out Mr. Brown; the rest of us want to go home." They were so drunk that they could not tell Mr. Brown from the rest of the men in the group, and they knew that Mrs. Brown would be able to find him.
